screens.title: Two models, two questions
screens.prose: This is López de Prado's **meta-labelling**, from *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*. A **primary** model picks the side. A **secondary** model is trained on the **meta-label**: 1 if the primary's trade hit its profit barrier, else 0. Its probability sets whether to trade, and how big.
screens.question: A long trade times out at the vertical barrier. What is its meta-label?

options.text: 0: it did not hit the profit barrier
1: it did not hit the stop either
options.why: You counted "not a loss" as a win. The meta-label is 1 only for a profit-barrier exit.
The meta-label has two values, 1 and 0. The side, not the meta-label, carries the sign.

hints.text: The meta-label asks one yes or no question.
This model learns it.
Yes means the trade reached its profit barrier. A time-out did not.

feedback.correct: Only a profit-barrier exit is a 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The meta-label is 1 only when the trade took its profit.

explain.text: The meta-label is binary: did acting on the primary pay? A time-out did not, so it is 0. The secondary never chooses the side; it only learns when the primary is worth following.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def primary_crossover_side(prices, fast, slow):
    p = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    sides = []
    for t in range(slow - 1, len(p)):   # the first day with a full slow window
        f = p[t - fast + 1:t + 1].mean()
        s = p[t - slow + 1:t + 1].mean()
        sides.append(1 if f > s else -1)
    return sides

explain.text: Both windows end at day $t$, so the side is known at the close of $t$, before any future close. A window ending at `t + 2` would peek one day ahead. The output is `slow - 1` shorter than the prices.

screens.title: Meta-labels in code
screens.prose: The triple-barrier labels of lesson 2 say which barrier the **price** hit: $+1$ upper, $-1$ lower, $0$ time. The side says which way we bet. Combine them into the meta-label.
screens.question: Complete `meta_labels` so it returns 1 where the trade hit its profit barrier and 0 otherwise.

widget.starter:
def meta_labels(sides, tb_labels):
    return [...]   # 1 where the trade hit its own profit barrier, else 0
widget.solution:
def meta_labels(sides, tb_labels):
    return [1 if s * y == 1 else 0 for s, y in zip(sides, tb_labels)]

screens.title: How good is the filter?
screens.prose: The secondary gives each trade a probability $p$. We act when $p$ is at least a threshold. **Precision**: of the trades we took, the share that paid. **Recall**: of the trades that paid, the share we took. Stat-learning lesson 12 met both.
screens.question: Complete `meta_precision_recall` so it returns (precision, recall), each rounded to 4 places.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def meta_precision_recall(y_meta, p, threshold):
    y = np.asarray(y_meta)
    p = np.asarray(p)
    take = p >= threshold           # the trades we act on
    precision = ...                 # share of taken trades that paid (0.0 if none taken)
    recall = ...                    # share of paying trades that we took
    return (round(float(precision), 4), round(float(recall), 4))
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def meta_precision_recall(y_meta, p, threshold):
    y = np.asarray(y_meta)
    p = np.asarray(p)
    take = p >= threshold           # the trades we act on
    precision = y[take].mean() if take.any() else 0.0
    recall = y[take].sum() / y.sum()
    return (round(float(precision), 4), round(float(recall), 4))

hints.text: `y[take]` keeps the meta-labels of the trades we took.
At 0.5 we take trades 1, 2 and 4.
`precision = y[take].mean() if take.any() else 0.0` and `recall = y[take].sum() / y.sum()`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Precision divides by trades taken; recall divides by trades that paid.

explain.text: On the seeded series' last 571 trades, a threshold of 0.5 gives precision 0.549 and recall 0.724. A threshold of 0 takes everything: recall 1, and precision 0.406, the primary's own hit rate. That base rate is what the filter must beat.

screens.title: Choosing a threshold
screens.prose: Raise the threshold and we trade less, with higher precision and lower recall. The **F1** score, $\frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}$, balances the two. The solid line is F1 on the test trades.
screens.question: Tap the threshold with the highest F1.

hints.text: Read the labels on the solid line.
Two points are close.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the highest point on the solid line.

byKey.t60: At 0.6 precision is higher, 0.677, but recall falls to 0.560, so F1 is 0.613.
byKey.t70: At 0.7 precision is high but only 29 trades remain: recall 0.086.
byKey.t30: At 0.3 nearly everything is taken: precision 0.418, close to the base rate.

explain.text: F1 is highest at 0.5, 0.625. A desk paying costs per trade may still prefer 0.6: 192 trades at 68% precision, not 306 at 55%. F1 is one way to choose, not the only one.

screens.title: What the 0.72 means
screens.prose: The primary says **short**. The secondary model gives this trade $p = 0.72$. A colleague reads it as "a 72% chance the price goes up". They conclude that the models disagree and the trade should be skipped.
screens.question: What does $p = 0.72$ say?

options.text: A 72% chance this short reaches its profit barrier, the lower one: take it
A 72% chance the price rises: skip the short
options.why: You read $p$ as the chance of a rise. The secondary was trained on meta-labels, so $p$ is the chance this call pays. For a short, paying means the price falls.
You turned $p$ into a statement about direction. It says nothing about the price alone, only about this call.

options.text: Nothing until we know the long trades' probabilities
options.why: Each probability stands alone: it rates this trade, with this side.

hints.text: What label was the secondary trained on?
The secondary never sees "up" or "down".
Its target was 1 when the primary's call paid. So $p$ is the chance the call pays.

feedback.correct: The secondary rates the call, not the price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the secondary's target: did the primary's trade pay?

byKey.up: You read $p$ as the chance of a rise. The secondary learned "does this call pay?", so 0.72 backs the short.

explain.text: The secondary's target was the meta-label, so $p$ estimates "this side pays". For a short that means the price falls to the lower barrier. Here $p = 0.72$ is a vote for the trade, and a large position.

widget.solution:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def fit_meta_model(X_train, y_meta_train, X_test):
    model = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_meta_train)
    p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    return [round(float(x), 4) for x in p]

screens.title: Side from one model, size from another
screens.prose:
With side $s_i$ from the primary and price label $y_i$ from the barriers, the meta-label is $$z_i = \mathbf{1}\{s_i y_i = 1\}.$$

The secondary estimates $p_i = P(z_i = 1 \mid \text{features})$. We trade $s_i$ when $p_i \ge c$, sized by $p_i$. At $c = 0$ we get the primary back.
screens.question: A primary is right on every training trade. What does the secondary learn?

options.text: Nothing useful: every meta-label is 1, so there is no 0 to tell apart

options.why: A filter needs bad trades to learn from. With every $z_i = 1$ there is only one class.
With one class, the fitted probability is 1 for every trade, whatever its volatility.

hints.text: List the meta-labels of a primary that is always right.

feedback.correct: One class leaves nothing to learn.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $z_i$ when every call pays.

explain.text: The secondary's job is to spot the primary's mistakes. With no mistakes, every $z_i$ is 1 and there is nothing to learn. With a primary that has no edge, the secondary must find all the edge itself, and usually cannot.

quiz.prose: A primary classifier is fitted on 2015 to 2019. A colleague then trains the secondary on the meta-labels of the primary's calls over the same years.
quiz.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: The primary was fitted to those years, so its calls look too good there; the secondary learns flattering meta-labels
Nothing: the secondary uses different features
options.why: Different features do not help. The meta-labels themselves are in-sample results of the primary.

options.text: The secondary has too little data
options.why: The size is the same either way. The trouble is that those calls are in-sample.

feedback.correct: Train the secondary on a later block the primary never saw.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the primary's calls on 2015 to 2019 are honest.

explain.text: In its own training years the primary looks skilled, so most meta-labels are 1. The secondary then learns a world that will not return. Fit the primary on one block, the secondary on the next, and test on a third.

quiz.prose: A primary picks its side by coin toss. On our six-year series about 35% of its calls reach the profit barrier.
quiz.question: What can meta-labelling add?

options.text: Little: the secondary would have to find all the edge alone, the hard problem we started with
It turns the coin into a good strategy
options.why: The secondary cannot choose sides. A coin's calls carry no information for it to filter.
Nothing guarantees that. The filter can only exploit patterns in when the coin happens to be right.

feedback.correct: Meta-labelling refines an edge; it does not create one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the secondary learn from, and what does a coin give it?

explain.text: The secondary learns when the primary is right. A coin is right at random, so the meta-labels track the price moves alone. The secondary is then a direction model in disguise, the problem meta-labelling was meant to avoid.

quiz.prose: Raising the secondary's threshold from 0.5 to 0.65.
quiz.question: What usually happens?

options.text: Fewer trades, higher precision, lower recall

options.why: A higher threshold keeps fewer trades, not more.
Recall can only fall as we drop trades: fewer winners are kept.

feedback.correct: A stricter filter trades less and more accurately.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A higher threshold keeps a subset of the trades.

explain.text: Every trade kept at 0.65 was kept at 0.5, so recall cannot rise. Precision usually rises, because the trades dropped had lower probabilities. On our test trades, 0.6 gave precision 0.677 on 192 trades.
